newsitem.title: BURUNDI: Fresh fighting, food shortage reported in Burundi.
newsitem.headline: Fresh fighting, food shortage reported in Burundi.

text.p: The civil war in Burundi, which has already killed 150,000 people, is spreading rapidly and causing widespread displacements of people and food shortages, a U.N. agency said on Saturday.
Earlier this week the Burundi army reported fighting just 15 km (eight miles) south of the capital Bujumbura.
The three-year-old civil war pits Burundi's Tutsi-led government against rebels drawn from the majority Hutu tribe.

"The conflict in Burundi, which has been somewhat overshadowed by the problems in eastern Zaire, is spreading rapidly and causing massive population displacements," the World Food Programme (WFP) said in a statement issued in Nairobi.

WFP said the regional committee of east African governments that imposed sanctions on Burundi after a military coup in July had given the agency clearance to take in enough food to feed 130,000 people.

It said the committee had cleared 2,545 tonnes of food a month to replenish its existing food stocks in Burundi, which are nearly exhausted. The agency will take the food by barge from the Tanzanian port of Kigoma on Lake Tanganyika or by truck across land from Tanzania.
Burundi's neighbours and some other African states imposed sanctions a week after Tutsi military leader Pierre Buyoya overthrew Hutu president Sylvestre Ntibantunganya on July 25.
Clashes between rebels and government forces have displaced tens of thousands of Burundians and 80,000 of them, twice as many as a few weeks ago, are now receiving food aid, it added.
About 50,000 refugees have returned from Zaire.

Fierce fighting was reported this week in Kabezi, 15 km (eight miles) south of Bujumbura, after rebels killed five civilians and two military personnel in Karongwe, 10 km (six miles) south of the capital, on Wednesday.
Army spokesman Isaie Nibizi, confirming the reports on Friday, said the army had encircled a rebel position at Kabezi, but gave no further details on the fighting.
Nibizi also said a priest had been lynched in Mubuga, 125 km (75 miles) from Bujumbura, "for spreading divisive teachings". He did not identify the priest but said an inquiry had been started.
Meanwhile, legal sources said Burundi's public prosecutor had stepped up a probe into a 1993 coup and the massacres that followed and charges could be laid before the end of the year.

President Melchior Ndadaye, a Hutu, was killed in the 1993 coup by Tutsi troops. His successor, Cyprien Ntaryamira, also a Hutu, died in the same plane crash that killed Rwandan President Juvenal Habyarimana in April 1994, sparking the genocide of Rwandan Tutsis and allied moderate Hutus by Hutu extremists.
Civilian and military suspects have been under investigation over the coup for two years, but have not been arrested.

The Hutu-dominated Frodebu (Front for Democracy in Burundi) party, to which Ndadaye belonged, called the probe a farce. Its spokesman, Frederic Bamvuginyuvira, said the military regime of Tutsi President Pierre Buyoya simply wanted to destroy Frodebu.
Several Frodebu officials are under investigation.
